_comment: Production series, film 2. Slides only (no recording); tables, code and query results from the complete example github.com/fundsxml/examples/tree/main/PostgreSQL_End_to_End.

description.en: How FundsXML data is stored in a database, with the complete PostgreSQL example of the FundsXML examples repository: the XML column and shredded tables, layers, a table model in which everything that repeats is a row (several funds per file, umbrellas and subfunds, several NAVs per day and currency, portfolios and positions, look-through), keys and assets without an ISIN, amounts and currencies, code lists, dates, transactions in four places, documents, regulatory templates, history and corrections, views, quality, access and performance. All files can be downloaded.

say.en: Where does the data of a FundsXML file live once it has arrived? In this film you see two ways of storing FundsXML in a database, a complete table model in which every repeating part of a file has its place, the traps around keys and currencies, and how to keep the history of deliveries and corrections. Everything you see comes from a complete example that you can download and run yourself.

items.head: Store the document
items.text: One XML column per file. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server can query it with XPath.

items.head: Shred into tables
items.text: One table per business object: fund, share class, price, position, asset.

items.head: Most setups: both
items.text: The original file, and the data you need in tables.

say.en: There are two basic ways. The first: store the whole document in an X M L column. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server all have one, and they can query it with X Path. The second: shred the document into tables, one per business object. Most setups do both: they keep the original file, and they load the data they need into tables.

en.title: Querying the XML column
en.code:
SELECT unique_document_id,
       cardinality(xpath('/FundsXML4/Funds/Fund', raw))     AS funds,
       cardinality(xpath('//Subfund', raw))                 AS subfunds,
       cardinality(xpath('//ShareClass/Prices/Price', raw)) AS prices
FROM delivery;

 unique_document_id                  funds  subfunds  prices
 EXAMPLE-AM-MONTHEND-2025-10-31          3         2     264
 EXAMPLE-AM-NAV-2025-11-05               3         2      66
 EXAMPLE-AM-DOCUMENTS-2025-11-03         0         0       0
 EXAMPLE-AM-NAV-2025-11-05-AMEND-1       3         2      66

say.en: Storing the document is simple and keeps everything, also data you do not use today. In the example, the deliveries table keeps every file in an X M L column, and a query counts the funds, subfunds and prices of each file directly with X Path. That is good for archives and for occasional questions, but slow for reporting over thousands of files.

items.head: XML column
items.text: Complete, queryable with XPath.

items.head: JSON column
items.text: Easier for web applications, but loses the order of elements and the difference between attributes and elements.

items.head: Always keep the original file
items.text: Unchanged: the record of what was received.

say.en: Some teams convert the file to J S O N and store that instead, because web applications like it. That works, but the conversion loses details: the order of elements and the difference between attributes and elements. Whatever you choose for daily use, keep the original file, unchanged, as the record of what was received.

items.head: Raw
items.text: delivery.raw: the file as received.

items.head: Staging
items.text: position_staging: waiting for the assets.

items.head: Core
items.text: Checked, own keys, history.

items.head: Reporting
items.text: Views for people and systems.

say.en: Many setups arrange the database in layers, and so does the example. The raw layer holds the original files, unchanged. The staging layer holds data as delivered, still unchecked: here, positions that wait for their assets. The core layer holds checked data with its own keys and the history. And the reporting layer offers views for the people and systems that use the data. Each layer has one job, and errors stay in the layer where they occur.

For daily work, tables are better. The model of the example follows the structure of FundsXML. Every delivery is registered first. Then come funds and, for umbrellas, their subfunds; share classes with their prices and net asset values; portfolios with their positions; the assets the positions refer to; the transactions; documents; and the regulatory templates. Twenty tables in all, in eight files.

en.title: The table definition
en.code:
CREATE TABLE fund (
    fund_id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    lei              text UNIQUE,
    name             text NOT NULL,
    currency         char(3) NOT NULL,
    parent_fund_id   bigint REFERENCES fund,     -- the umbrella of a subfund
    single_fund_flag boolean);
CREATE TABLE share_class (
    share_class_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    fund_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES fund, isin char(12) NOT NULL UNIQUE, ...);
CREATE TABLE price (
    share_class_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES share_class,
    nav_date date NOT NULL, nature text NOT NULL,      -- OFFICIAL, ESTIMATED
    nav_price numeric NOT NULL, currency char(3) NOT NULL,
    delivery_id bigint NOT NULL, replaced_by_delivery_id bigint);

say.en: Here is the table definition. The columns follow the FundsXML elements, so that the mapping stays easy to read: the fund has its L E I, its name, its currency and, for a subfund, the umbrella it belongs to. The share class has its I S I N and the fund. A price row has the share class, the date, the nature of the price, the value, and the delivery it came from.

en.title: Everything that repeats is a row

say.en: The most important rule of the model: everything that can repeat in a file is a row, never a column. A file can carry several funds. A fund has several share classes. A share class has prices for many dates, and on one date an estimated and an official price. Net assets come in several currencies. A fund has portfolios for many dates, each with hundreds of positions. Whoever puts a second date or a second currency into columns rebuilds the table with the next delivery.

Here is what the example deliveries bring. The month-end file holds four funds: an umbrella with two subfunds, and two single funds, so five rows in the fund table. Together that is twenty-four valuation days, two hundred sixty-four prices and five hundred twenty-two positions, in one file. The daily file brings three days, each with an estimated and an official value.

en.title: One share class, one day: four rows
en.note: nav: Multi Asset Opportunities Fund, CHF class, 2025-11-05

say.en: One share class on one day shows why. The franc class of the multi-asset fund reports its net assets as an estimate and as the official value, each in francs and in euros, flagged as share-class currency and as fund currency. Four rows, one day, one share class. A table with one value column per day could not hold them.

en.title: One position on its way into a table
en.code:
<Position>
  <UniqueID>MA_0014</UniqueID>                    only valid inside this file
  <Identifiers><ISIN>IEXMPLS00036</ISIN></Identifiers>
  <TotalValue><Amount ccy="EUR">10364653.57</Amount></TotalValue>
  <TotalPercentage>3.7177</TotalPercentage>
  <ShareClass><Shares>50287</Shares> ...</ShareClass>
</Position>

position:
 portfolio  no  look_through  asset  position_type  total_value  ccy  percentage  quantity
         3  48  false           346  ShareClass     10364653.57  EUR      3.7177     50287
 portfolio 3 = Example Multi Asset Opportunities Fund, 2025-10-31, delivery 1

say.en: Here is one position on its way into a table. At the top, in the file: the sender's reference to the asset, the total value with its currency, and the weight. Below, the row: the asset is now the key of the database; the value keeps its currency; the row knows its portfolio, and through it the fund, the date and the delivery. And it keeps its number in the file, so that a generator can write the positions back in the same order.

items.head: PositionsDecomposed
items.text: The holdings of the target funds of a fund of funds.

items.head: Same table, one flag
items.text: position.look_through = true: 73 rows in the example.

items.head: Not counted twice
items.text: Reconciliation uses the fund's own positions only.

say.en: A fund of funds can also deliver what its target funds hold: the look-through. These positions have the same shape as the fund's own, so they go into the same table, with a flag. The example has seventy-three of them. The flag matters: the reconciliation counts only the fund's own positions, never the look-through as well.

items.head: SingleFundFlag true
items.text: Share classes directly under the fund.

items.head: SingleFundFlag false
items.text: Subfunds, each with its own share classes.

items.head: One table
items.text: A parent column: queries do not need to know the kind of fund.

say.en: One structural point: single funds and umbrellas. FundsXML says with the single fund flag whether a fund has share classes directly, or subfunds that each have their own share classes. In the database, one fund table with a parent column handles both cases. In the example, the umbrella and its two subfunds are three rows of the same table, and queries do not need to know which kind of fund they look at.

items.head: UniqueID is only valid inside one file
items.text: The next delivery may use it for another security.

items.head: Own keys
items.text: Based on ISIN, LEI or the sender's own codes.

items.head: Resolved while loading
items.text: The position is linked to our asset.

say.en: One trap concerns keys. A position points to its asset through the Unique ID. But that ID is only valid inside one file: the next delivery may use the same ID for another security. So the database needs its own keys, based on the ISIN, the LEI or the sender's own codes, and the link between position and asset is resolved while loading.

items.head: A built key
items.text: Sender + type of asset + sender's own ID.

items.head: All identifiers in their own table
items.text: ISIN, WKN, Bloomberg ticker, internal codes.

say.en: And not every asset has an I S I N. Cash accounts, over-the-counter derivatives and currency forwards usually have none; in the example, forty-five of four hundred thirty assets. For them, build a key from the sender, the type of asset and the sender's own identifier. Keep all identifiers of an asset in a table of their own, so that any of them can be used to find it.

items.head: One amount, several currencies
items.text: Flags for the fund and the share-class currency.

items.head: Store the currency with every amount
items.text: If needed, several rows per amount.

items.head: Never a bare number
items.text: The most common source of wrong reports.

say.en: Amounts are the next trap, as the franc class showed. In FundsXML, one amount can be given in several currencies at once, with flags for the fund currency and the share-class currency. So the database stores the currency with every amount, keeps the flags, and writes several rows where needed. A bare number without its currency is the most common source of wrong reports.

items.head: Fixed lists in the schema
items.text: Document types, price types, data operations, ...

items.head: Lookup tables
items.text: Filled from the schema, refreshed with every version.

items.head: Checked and readable
items.text: Incoming codes checked, readable names in reports.

say.en: Many FundsXML elements use fixed lists of codes: document types, price natures, data operations and many more. Store them in lookup tables, filled from the schema, and refresh them with every new version. In the example, a small script reads the lists from the schema file and writes them into a code list table, per schema version. Then the database can check incoming codes, and reports can show readable names.

items.head: ContentDate
items.text: The day the data is valid for.

items.head: DocumentGenerated
items.text: When the file was written.

items.head: NavDate
items.text: The valuation day of a price.

items.head: Store all three
items.text: And decide which one reports use.

say.en: Dates need care too. A file has a content date, the day its data is valid for, and a generation time, when it was written. A price has its own date, the valuation day. These can all differ: a file generated on Monday morning carries prices of Friday. Store all of them, and decide clearly which one your reports use.

items.head: Flows
items.text: Subscriptions, redemptions: sc_flow, 67 rows.

items.head: Distributions
items.text: Per share class: distribution, 3 rows.

items.head: Trades
items.text: The fund's own: trade, 209 rows.

items.head: Income
items.text: Dividends, coupons, interest: earning, 68 rows.

say.en: Transactions live in four places in FundsXML, and the model keeps them apart. Subscriptions, redemptions and distributions belong to a share class. The fund's own trades and its income belong to the portfolio of a date. The month-end file of the example brings sixty-seven flows, three distributions, two hundred nine trades and sixty-eight income records. Trades keep their complete X M L next to the columns, so nothing of a complex trade is lost.

Documents get a table of their own. A document is either a link, then the table keeps the address, or it is embedded, then the table keeps the decoded file itself, with its size and a hash to recognise it again. A second table says which funds and share classes a document belongs to; one key information document can apply to several share classes, in several languages. A function returns the documents in force on any day.

en.title: Regulatory templates: XML plus key fields
en.note: regulatory_report: plus the whole template record as XML

say.en: Regulatory templates are a world of their own: hundreds of fields each, and a new version every few years. The example keeps every template record in one table: the template, its version, the share class, the record as X M L, and the few fields it reports on as columns, such as the ongoing costs of the E M T or the S F D R product type of the E E T. Avoid one column per field and version; it ends in confusion.

items.head: Every row knows its delivery
items.text: Document ID and content date.

items.head: AMEND replaces, DELETE removes
items.text: Of the delivery it names.

items.head: Nothing is overwritten
items.text: Old rows are marked as replaced.

say.en: Data changes, and corrections arrive. So every row remembers where it came from: the delivery, its document ID, and the content date, the date the data is valid for. A delivery with the data operation amend replaces the values of an earlier one; delete removes them. The original rows are not overwritten, they are marked as replaced.

en.title: NAV of the CHF class: today and as known before

say.en: This makes questions like these simple: what was the net asset value of the franc class on the fourth of November, as known today, and as known on the morning of the sixth, before the correction arrived? The correction changed one value. Both versions are in the table, and the query picks the one that was valid.

items.head: One view per use
items.text: current_price, current_nav, latest_portfolio, current_position.

items.head: A function for documents
items.text: documents_in_force(day).

items.head: History hidden, names stable
items.text: Tables can change underneath.

say.en: Users should not have to know how the history works. Offer views for each use: the current prices, the current net assets, the latest portfolio per fund, the documents in force. The views hide the logic of deliveries and replaced rows, and give consumers stable names. Then you can change the tables underneath without breaking every report that reads them.

items.head: A status per delivery
items.text: loaded, checked, released.

items.head: Findings per delivery
items.text: delivery_finding: rule, path, value, message.

items.head: Who released, when
items.text: release_delivery().

say.en: Store the quality of the data with the data. Each delivery has a status: loaded, checked or released. The findings of the checks are stored with it: the rule, the place in the file, the value found. A function releases a checked delivery and records who did it, and when. The views show released data only, and anyone can see why a value was held back.

en.title: Access: each client sees its own

say.en: Portfolios are confidential. A data vendor or an insurer may hold the portfolios of many clients in one database, and each client may only see its own. So separate the roles of loading, releasing and reading, and control access per client. The example does it with row-level security: a reader for the insurer sees the one fund its client may see, and nothing else.

items.head: Positions grow fastest
items.text: Thousands per fund and month.

items.head: Indexes
items.text: ISIN, date, delivery.

say.en: A few words on performance. Positions grow fastest: thousands per fund and month. Index the columns you search by: ISIN, date and delivery. Partition large tables by month. And load in bulk instead of row by row. With these measures, ordinary databases handle many years of FundsXML deliveries without trouble.

en.headline: Start with what you use.
en.sub: Keep the original file next to it, and add tables when new needs come up.

say.en: A last piece of advice: do not model the whole schema at once. Start with the data you really use, keep the original file next to it, and add tables when new needs come up. The schema has thousands of elements, and most companies use a small part of them.

items.head: ddl/
items.text: Tables, views, access, code lists.

items.head: loader/, generator/
items.text: The loader and the generator of the next films.

items.head: data/
items.text: Six deliveries, four bad files, the generated files.

items.head: run_all.sh
items.text: Everything, end to end.

say.en: Everything you saw in this film is in the complete example: the table definitions, the views and the access rules, the code lists, the sample deliveries, the loader and the generator. You find it in the FundsXML examples repository on GitHub, in the folder PostgreSQL end to end, also as a single zip file. One script builds the database, loads the files and runs every query of this film.

That was FundsXML in a database: documents and tables, everything that repeats as rows, keys, amounts and codes, and history. In the next film, you load the example deliveries into this model. Thanks for watching.
